items.reasoning: Assumption 1 says the development of agricultural technology is confined to developed countries, but the passage says only that 'much of this change is brought about by affluent farmers in the West/Americas' — 'much of' deliberately leaves room for change originating elsewhere, so 'confined to' overstates it. Assumption 2 says agricultural technology is not adapted in developing countries, and the passage contradicts it directly: 'Techniques developed in the West are being adapted in some places to make tropical crops more productive.' Both are absolutes the passage qualifies, so neither is valid.

items.value: Assumption 1 only — poor countries need to change their existing farming techniques
items.reasoning: The passage says technology is of little use unless adapted, and that in the developing world this 'applies as much to existing farming techniques as it does to the latest advances in genetic modification'; it then argues that extending best current practice to the smallholders of Africa and Asia, in matters as simple as how much fertilizer to apply and when, would greatly increase food availability. That is assumption 1. Assumption 2 compares developed countries' infrastructure and wastage with others, a comparison the passage never draws — it says only that better roads and storage would reduce wastage, without saying who currently has them.

items.value: Assumption 1 only — growing enough food for future generations will be a challenge
items.reasoning: The passage opens with staple yields having plateaued, new strains and agrochemicals no longer raising them, little suitable unfarmed land left, and rising temperatures set to make some places unfit for farming — that is exactly the assumption that feeding future generations will be a challenge. Corporate farming is not mentioned anywhere in the passage; its remedies are adaptation of technology, better agronomic practice for smallholders, and better roads and storage. So assumption 2 is not valid.

In a row of five positions, exactly two letters lie between A and E when their positions differ by 3, i.e. the pairs (1,4) and (2,5). Each pair can be filled in two ways (A first or E first), giving 4 placements of A and E. The remaining three letters B, C and D fill the remaining three seats in 3! = 6 ways. Total 4 x 6 = 24.

items.value: Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient
items.reasoning: Statement 1 tells us that X is male and that Y is male, but says nothing about Z's sex — 'Y is a brother of Z' fixes Y's sex, not Z's, so Z may be X's sister. Statement 2 establishes only that the three are siblings, again without any sex. Combining them still leaves Z's sex unknown, so it cannot be settled whether Z is X's brother.

The road is 1.01 km = 1010 m and carries 101 plants at equal spacing, so with plants at both ends there are 101 - 1 = 100 gaps, each 1010 / 100 = 10.1 m. Five consecutive plants span four gaps, so the total distance between the first and the fifth is 4 x 10.1 = 40.4 m. The distractor 40 m comes from wrongly taking the spacing as 10 m, which would need 102 plants to cover 1010 m.

Journeys from A to C fall into two mutually exclusive kinds. Going via B, there are 3 roads from A to B and 4 from B to C, giving 3 x 4 = 12 routes. Going directly, there are 3 roads from A to C. Since the two kinds cannot overlap, the totals add: 12 + 3 = 15.

Work backwards from D, who ends with the smallest two-digit number, 10. C gave half his coins plus 2 more, so half of C's holding plus 2 equals 10, giving C 16. Likewise half of B's holding plus 2 equals 16, giving B 28, and half of A's holding plus 2 equals 28, giving A 52. Checking forwards: A has 52 and gives 26 + 2 = 28 to B; B gives 14 + 2 = 16 to C; C gives 8 + 2 = 10 to D.

The series is made of blocks A, AB, ABC, ABCD, ... where the nth block has n letters, so the blocks end at cumulative positions n(n+1)/2: 1, 3, 6, 10, ... The 13th block ends at 13 x 14 / 2 = 91 and the 14th block, ABCDEFGHIJKLMN, occupies positions 92 to 105. Position 100 is the 100 - 91 = 9th letter of that block, which is I.

Counting from the front, C stands 12th because 11 people are ahead of him. Seven people between B and C means their positions differ by 8, so B is 4th or 20th. Four people between A and B means their positions differ by 5. If B is 4th then A is 9th (the alternative is off the queue), and since 13 stand behind A the queue has 9 + 13 = 22. If B is 20th, A is 15th or 25th, giving 28 or 38. All three are consistent, so the minimum is 22, and the check holds: with 22 in the queue, B is 4th, A 9th (4 between them) and C 12th (7 between B and C), with 11 ahead of C and 13 behind A.

Statement 1 restates the passage: organisms 'can never be fully prepared for environmental catastrophes that await life' and an outcome is the extinction of those that cannot overcome the adversity. Statement 3 is the passage's own explanation, that the failure to survive is 'attributed to the genomes which are unable to withstand geological vagaries or biological mishaps'. Statement 4 is supported by 'extinction of species has been a major feature'. Statement 2 fails on the word 'all': the passage says over 90% of species that have ever lived are now extinct, while up to ten million still exist, so it never claims that all existing species will die out. Only option C excludes statement 2.

items.value: Because no evidence has ever refuted it
items.reasoning: The author calls it more than a theory because it has the standing of established fact: 'Evolution happens — this is a fact', the mechanism 'is amply supported by scientific data', and 'to date no single zoological, botanical, geological, paleontological, genetic or physical evidence has refuted either of the central two main Darwinian ideas'. That is option C. Option A inverts the passage, which faults creationist doctrine rather than Darwin; option B states a finding of the theory, not a reason for its status; option D is the creationist position the passage rejects.

items.value: Assumption 1 only — only species able to overcome environmental catastrophes will survive and perpetuate
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 is the converse of the passage's own claim that extinction befalls 'those species which cannot overcome environmental adversity', so it is valid. Assumption 2 misreads the figure: the passage says more than 90% of species that have ever lived are already extinct, not that more than 90% of species now on earth are in danger. Assumption 3 overstates the closing comparison — the passage says Darwinian laws are acceptable alongside those of Copernicus, Galileo, Newton and Einstein as sets of natural laws, not that Darwin's theory explains all natural phenomena. Only option A keeps 1 and drops both 2 and 3.

items.value: Water management practices in India need to change dramatically in the coming years
items.reasoning: Water is the thread that ties the whole passage together: middle-class affluence has shifted diets towards milk, fish and meat, 'all of which need significantly more water to produce than cereal-based diets', while more gadgets and vehicles need more energy and 'generation of energy needs water'. Both consequences of prosperity converge on rising water demand, which is option D. Option A prescribes persuading people back to cereal diets, which the passage never suggests; option B reads the passage as a call for more production when it is describing a strain; option C picks up the technology detail while missing the water conclusion the passage builds to. The judgement call is that the passage states a trend and no prescription at all, so D is an inference from it rather than a restatement — but it is the only option that follows the water thread the passage builds.

Convert each unit to seconds: a week is 7 x 24 x 3600 = 604800 s, a day 86400 s, an hour 3600 s, a minute 60 s and a second 1 s. With x of each, the total is x(604800 + 86400 + 3600 + 60 + 1) = 694861x. The distractor 694860x drops the x seconds themselves.

items.value: T is the granddaughter of Q
items.reasoning: P's daughter is T and U is T's mother, so P and U are one couple and T and S are their daughters. R's son is P, and R is Q's spouse, so R and Q are the second couple and are P's parents, hence T's grandparents. T is called a daughter, so T is female and is therefore Q's granddaughter, making option D certain. Options A and B cannot both be settled because the passage never fixes whether Q is the grandfather or the grandmother, and for the same reason option C is unsettled — 'R's son is P' fixes P's sex, not R's.

items.value: Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient
items.reasoning: Statement 1 gives only the Q-R distance and statement 2 only the P-R distance, so neither alone says anything about P to Q. Together they fix two sides of a triangle but not the angle between them, so the P-Q distance can be anything from 43 - 18 = 25 km (P, Q and R collinear with Q between) to 43 + 18 = 61 km (collinear with R between). Since the distance is not determined, both statements together are insufficient.

From 'all pens are books' and 'no chair is a pen', chairs are excluded from the pens but nothing fixes their relation to books. Conclusion I fails because chairs need not be books at all. Conclusion II directly contradicts the second statement, which denies any overlap between chairs and pens. Conclusion III reverses the first statement, which does not permit conversion — books may include things that are not pens and need not be chairs. Conclusion IV fails because a chair may well be a book that happens not to be a pen, which is consistent with both statements. Hence none follows.

Take the doctors who are teachers, which the first statement guarantees exist. All teachers are engineers, so those doctors are engineers, which makes Conclusion III ('some engineers are doctors') true. All engineers are scientists, so those same people are scientists, which makes Conclusion I ('some scientists are doctors') true. Conclusion II is a universal claim that does not follow, since nothing forces every engineer to be a doctor — the overlap established is only partial.

items.value: None of the above — none of the three statements is forced by the conditions
items.reasoning: Reading 'in between' as sitting immediately between, E-A-D and B-F-H are each blocks of three consecutive seats, leaving C and G in the two remaining seats, with B and D barred from the seats adjacent to and opposite C. Enumerating all seatings that satisfy this gives six distinct arrangements up to rotation: ADGBFHCE, ADGCHFBE, ADHFBGCE, AEBFHCGD, AECGBFHD and AECHFBGD. B is never between A and G in any of them, so option A is false outright. C sits opposite G in only two of the six and E sits opposite F in only two, so neither option B nor option C is definitely correct. For instance ADGCHFBE satisfies every condition while making all three statements false. Hence none of the above.
